analysis.one_liner: Restores expired taxes on polluting companies to fund toxic waste cleanup and oil spill response.
analysis.headline: The bill to reinstate Superfund and oil spill taxes died in the Senate Finance Committee with no vote and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1995, companies that make hazardous substances and crude oil no longer pay the fees that once financed Superfund toxic waste cleanups; taxpayers have covered the bill instead. This bill would have brought back those fees — a per-barrel tax on crude oil, a tax on hazardous chemical feedstocks, a leaking storage tank tax, and a minimum tax on large corporations — through 2012, and raised the oil spill fund's exemption threshold from $1 billion to $5 billion.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who have paid Superfund cleanup costs out of general revenues since the polluter fees lapsed in 1995, and communities near toxic waste sites whose cleanups would be funded by the industries responsible for the contamination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate through September 30, 2012, restoring the principle that the companies whose chemicals created toxic sites help pay for their cleanup.

Reinstates the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund financing rate through 2012 and raises the unobligated-balance exemption from $1 billion to $5 billion, so the fund that pays oil spill damages is replenished by a per-barrel tax on crude oil.
Extends the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund financing rate through October 1, 2012, funding cleanup of gasoline leaks from storage tanks.
Reinstates the Corporate Environmental Income Tax (a corporate minimum tax) through tax years beginning before January 1, 2012, adding a revenue source tied to corporate activity.

analysis.who_pays: Petroleum companies, hazardous chemical manufacturers, and large corporations, which would pay the excise fees and the environmental minimum tax; some of the per-barrel oil tax could be passed through to consumers in fuel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, chemical, and large corporate taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on crude oil are commonly passed through to consumers, so part of the cost of refilling the oil spill fund could show up at the gas pump.

The corporate environmental income tax is a parallel minimum tax on corporations, which critics generally describe as adding compliance complexity and raising business costs, some of which can be passed on.
The bill only extends the taxes through 2012 and does not by itself guarantee that the money is spent faster on cleanups; slow site remediation depends on appropriations, not just fund balances.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: shifting Superfund and oil spill funding from general taxpayers back to the polluting industries. The main honest cost is that petroleum taxes reach consumers indirectly through fuel prices, and the minimum tax adds complexity. On the whole the bill would move a cleanup burden off general taxpayers and onto the companies whose products created it, which is a favorable trade for most people.

outcome.mechanism: The Finance Committee chairman introduced it the day after referring it to his own committee, and it sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Baucus, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, introduced the bill on September 17, 2002, near the end of the 107th Congress.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action was taken.
The bill drew no cosponsors and never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum, chemical, and large corporate taxpayers are better off, because the Superfund cleanup burden stayed on general taxpayers and the industry fees remained lapsed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and chemical companies; taxpayers kept paying cleanup

for.name: Sen. Max Baucus
for.role: Senator from Montana and Chairman, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the Superfund, oil spill, storage tank, and corporate environmental taxes.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition never appeared in the record.

industries.note: The bill reinstates a per-barrel tax on domestic and imported crude oil to refill the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund and fund Superfund. Since the tax lapsed in 1995, the industry has not paid these fees and general taxpayers have covered cleanup costs instead.
The bill restores the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate on chemical feedstocks, which lapsed in 1995. Without it, taxpayers fund the cleanup of sites contaminated by these industries.
The bill reinstates the Corporate Environmental Income Tax, a minimum tax on corporations, through 2012. It adds a tax burden that did not apply while lapsed.
Replenished trust funds would support more funded cleanup of Superfund sites, oil spills, and leaking storage tanks, which is work performed by the remediation industry.
